The Cuban Missile Crisis. In October nineteen sixty-two, a thirteen-day confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union unfolded during the Cold War over the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, just ninety miles from American shores. The crisis brought the world closer to nuclear war than any other Cold War moment. Resolution required secret negotiations, careful brinkmanship, and American concessions regarding Jupiter missiles in Turkey that remained publicly hidden for decades.

President John F. Kennedy and his national security team learned on October sixteenth, nineteen sixty-two, that reconnaissance photographs from U-2 spy planes had detected Soviet intermediate-range ballistic missiles being installed in Cuba under the direction of Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev. Khrushchev had secretly deployed the missiles to protect Fidel Castro's revolutionary Cuban regime from American invasion following the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in nineteen sixty-one and to address a perceived American nuclear advantage over the Soviet Union.

Kennedy convened the Executive Committee of senior advisors, including Robert Kennedy, his brother and Attorney General, Dean Rusk, Robert McNamara, and military leaders. The group debated military strikes versus naval blockade versus diplomacy. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine, or blockade, of Cuba on October twenty-second, escalating tensions as Soviet ships approached the American interdiction line. The two superpowers engaged in high-stakes brinkmanship with nuclear war seemingly imminent.

Nikita Khrushchev backed down on October twenty-eighth, announcing removal of the missiles from Cuba. Kennedy had secretly agreed to remove American Jupiter missiles from Turkey, kept secret for decades to avoid appearing weak and to protect American credibility. The crisis demonstrated both the real risk of nuclear war and the capacity of superpowers to negotiate crises. It led to the Hot Line agreement establishing a direct Kennedy-Khrushchev communication channel and contributed to the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty in nineteen sixty-three.
